Re: Docket No. PF26-11-000

    Draft Resource Reports 1-3, 5-10, and 12

Dear Secretary Reese:

        On June 17, 2026, in the above docketed proceeding, the Director of the Office of Energy
Projects (OEP) issued a letter order granting a request by Cook Inlet LNG, LLC (CILNG) to initiate
the NEPA pre-filing review process for the Cook Inlet LNG Project under 18 C.F.R. §157.21 of the
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) regulations.

        CILNG herein submits the draft of Resource Reports 1-3, 5-10, and 12 pursuant to Sections
157.21(f)(10) & (12) of the Commission’s regulations.

       Should you have any questions about this submission, please feel free to contact me at (202)
331-3185 or Corri Feige at (907) 232-1192.

1.    RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION
1.1   INTRODUCTION
Cook Inlet LNG, LLC (“CILNG” or the “Applicant”), a limited liability company organized under the laws of
the State of Delaware, proposes to construct and operate the Cook Inlet LNG Project (the “Project”), a Floating
Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU)-based natural gas import terminal located approximately two miles
offshore of the West Foreland in Cook Inlet, Alaska. This location is within State of Alaska waters of Cook Inlet
and is not on the U.S. Outer Continental Shelf nor under the jurisdiction of Bureau of Ocean Energy Management
or Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement. The Project will be owned and operated by CILNG.

The Project is designed to maximize the reuse of existing oil and gas infrastructure in Cook Inlet. The Applicant
will convert the existing Osprey Platform, an oil and gas production platform in continuous operation since 2002,
to receive regasified LNG as vaporous natural gas from an FSRU. Vaporous natural gas will be transferred to
shore through existing subsea and onshore pipelines. The Project requires only a mooring system for the FSRU
and limited pipeline upgrades to support Project throughput. No new offshore platform or greenfield onshore
LNG terminal facilities are proposed.

On June 1, 2026, the Applicant requested approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
the Commission) to commence the Commission's pre-filing review process pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 157.21,
following an initial consultation with the Commission's Office of Energy Projects on January 29, 2026. The
Applicant anticipates filing an application for authorization under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act (15 U.S.C.
§ 717b) in December 2026, requesting Commission authorization no later than August 2027, with an anticipated
in-service date in the third quarter of 2029.

Given the Project's limited scope, including its re-purposing of existing infrastructure, its limited footprint and
environmental impact, the Applicant proposes to prepare and file an Applicant-Prepared Draft Environmental
Assessment (APDEA), to be prepared by the Applicant's environmental contractor, Fairweather, LLC, and sub-
contractor Fairweather Science, LLC, in accordance with the Commission's 2011 Guidance for Applicant-
Prepared Draft Environmental Assessments.

This Resource Report 1 describes the Project and its purpose and need from a local, regional, and statewide
perspective, and, in accordance with 18 C.F.R. § 380.12, discusses facility layout and design, construction
methods, land and marine area requirements, non-jurisdictional facilities, and applicable regulatory approvals.
1.2   PURPOSE AND NEED
Natural gas serves as a key energy source for Southcentral Alaska. This has been true since the 1950’s, when
low-cost gas was available as a by-product of oil produced in the Cook Inlet. Natural gas is consumed by
industrial users such as the regional refinery, by commercial facilities (businesses, government, and non-
governmental users), and by regional utilities for both power generation and consumer heating service. Alaska
Department of Natural Resources (AKDNR) estimates [1] that from 2016 to 2021, gas demand averaged 68
billion cubic feet (Bcf) per year and that this demand was roughly comprised of 21% commercial, 35%
electricity, 28% for residential, and 15% for oil and gas operations.
In early 2022, Cook Inlet producers announced that, in the future, they would no longer be able to support long-
term supply contracts as reserves were insufficient. Shortly thereafter, regional utilities and the State of Alaska
formed a working group to address the issue and studies determined that significant supply shortfalls could begin
as early as 2029 and certainly by 2031.

1.3.2   PROJECT FACILITY COMPONENT LISTING
The Project's proposed facilities consist of the following primary components:

Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) – (Non-Jurisdictional 2)
The Project will utilize an FSRU moored on a long-term basis south-southwest of the Osprey Platform. The
FSRU itself is expected to provide a peak sendout capacity of at least 300 MMscfd, a guaranteed N+1 capacity
of at least 200 MMscfd, and a minimum stable sendout of approximately 50 MMscfd. The Project design will

Under the current utilization assumptions, cargo deliveries will occur every 30 to 45 days on average.

While the ultimate FSRU charterer has yet to be selected, the FSRU is anticipated to be a membrane-type
carrier with a length of 289 meters, a breadth of 46 meters and a design draft of 11.5 meters.

the FSRU, with six anchor chains running to each buoy. The system additionally employs eight anchor chains
fastened to submerged hard points near the bilge keels of the FSRU to improve transverse restraint. This
arrangement was selected because it effectively manages the environmental conditions at the project location
while minimizing environmental impact. An illustration of the proposed mooring system in show in Figure 3.

Regasification and Gas Transfer System
Regasified natural gas will be transferred from the FSRU to the Osprey Platform via a high-pressure flexible
transfer hose suspended above the water surface, to prevent interference from periodic ice in the area. The final
configuration will be aligned with the finalized mooring design accounting for the actual separation distance
between the FSRU and Osprey Platform. Currently, the separation distance is contemplated to be 100m –
120m.

The FSRU will use a closed loop regasification system. A block diagram of the proposed regasification circuit
is provided in Appendix C. In a closed loop regasification system on an FSRU, liquid natural gas is warmed
back into a vaporous phase using a recirculating intermediate fluid, typically a water-glycol mixture. The
intermediate fluid is heated on board by steam boilers or heat recovery systems, and it transfers that heat to the
cold LNG in a heat exchanger. The intermediate fluid is then continually recirculated to be reheated without
discharging water into the sea. This is a common system used in cold water environments like Cook Inlet.
The gas transfer system, as vessel-based equipment integral to the non-jurisdictional FSRU, is not itself subject
to the Commission's jurisdiction. FERC jurisdiction over the project facilities will commence at the receiving
interface at the Osprey Platform's gas connection point, where the flexible, high-pressure gas transfer line
connects to the platform.

Osprey Platform Conversion
The existing Osprey Platform will be converted to receive high-pressure natural gas from the FSRU’s gas
transfer system at the platform's gas receiving point. The FSRU maintains its own independent mooring
system and is not moored to the platform itself.

Conversion of the Osprey Platform and onshore facilities from oil production to natural gas throughput will
include removal and disposal of existing oil production equipment, including separators, treaters, and produced
water handling systems. The platform deck will be cleaned and decontaminated in preparation for gas service.
The platform’s eight existing production wells (seven in Leg 3, one in Leg 2) will be plugged and abandoned
to Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) standards using the platform's existing cranes
with coil tubing or a snubbing unit, without the need for a drilling rig.

Pipeline System
Natural gas will travel from the Osprey Platform through existing subsea and onshore pipelines to a custody
transfer meter located near the existing onshore Trading Bay Production facilities, then onward into the
regional pipeline system (West Cook Inlet Gas Gathering System (CIGGS)) owned by Harvest Midstream. A
study of this pipeline system using hydraulic modeling was performed by Coffman Engineers, Inc. to evaluate
capacity, identify system bottlenecks, and identify areas of questionable integrity.
The Coffman study indicates the existing pipeline system, while complying with a current maximum operating

Hydrostatic Testing and Water Sources
Hydrostatic testing of existing and any new pipeline segments will be required for the Project as a part of the
PHMSA Conversion of Service process under 49 CFR Part 192. Based upon past operational experience at the
Project location, approximately 3000 barrels of testing fluid has been required for testing the entire length of
pipeline from Osprey Platform to MOS. All fluid for hydrostatic testing will be sourced from an existing, lined
water storage area near WMR. If other makeup water is required, use of surface water from a nearby non-
perennial pond would be authorized by ADNR under a Temporary Water Use Authorization, as is the current
practice for oil production operations. All hydrostatic test water will be recycled and reused in the process to the
maximum extent possible. Upon completion of testing, hydrostatic testing fluids will be disposed of through an
existing EPA Class I non-hazardous disposal well located at WMR which the Project will own and operate. No
use of off-site water sources is anticipated for the Project. A final hydrostatic testing plan will be developed once
final pipeline engineering and construction planning is complete. A full hydrostatic testing plan complete with
procedures, planned water sources and any test water additives will be outlined and provided.
The Project is not anticipated to require substantial water for any aspect of the operation beyond hydrostatic
testing. The existing oil production operator currently holds a TWUA (#A2022-71) through the ADNR for
industrial uses such as oil and gas development operations and drilling, maintenance including hydrostatic
testing, pad construction and maintenance, and dust control. The total allowable take under that TWUA from
five separate surface lakes is 92,000,350 gallons maximum per year for five years, with a daily limit of no more
than 680,000 gallons. Additionally, KPF and WMR both have existing water supply wells for domestic water
needs in support of personnel camps and offices.
The Project water use will be minimal as the Project does not require water for pad construction, drilling or oil
production, only for limited seasonal dust control on the gravel road. The WMR man camp will be used in
support of construction operations and then be idled for normal Project operations. KPF has a small office facility
with crew quarters that will be used for two onshore personnel to manage road maintenance and general facility
upkeep. No estimate of water use outside of hydrostatic testing is available at this time but will be developed as
the overall construction schedule is completed and man camp utilization is calculated.

monitoring, and installation and maintenance of erosion and sediment controls (i.e. silt fence, straw wattle, slope
breakers, sediment barriers). EIs will have authority, consistent with Plan, to stop any activity that violates

1.6.1   OPERATIONS
Under normal operating conditions, the Project is designed to provide throughput at rates commensurate with
customer needs and specifications and will be in continuous operation. Normal operations include periodic
receipt of LNG cargoes via STS transfer, continuous regasification and gas delivery to the downstream pipeline
system, monitoring and control of pressure and flow, and routine inspection and surveillance of critical systems.
LNG storage on the FSRU, regasification, and onboard utilities will be operated under vessel-based control
consistent with marine and class requirements applicable to the FSRU.

Following conversion of the existing pipeline system to natural gas service, pipeline operations will be governed
by 49 C.F.R. Part 192, Subpart L. This requires the development and implementation of written operations and
maintenance procedures in accordance with 49 C.F.R. § 192.605, continuous monitoring and pressure control of
the pipeline system, regular leak surveys with prompt correction of identified hazardous conditions, and proper
recordkeeping and documentation of operational activities. Personnel performing operations tasks on the
converted pipeline system will be required to meet operator qualification standards under 49 C.F.R. Part 192,
Subpart N. Onshore operations will be supported by retained facilities at KPF and WMR (see Figure 5 and Figure
7).

Operating procedures will address safe marine operations and vessel movements, LNG handling and gas transfer
activities, emergency response and abnormal operating conditions, and environmental monitoring and reporting
requirements. Emergency response plans and drills will be developed and maintained to ensure preparedness for
credible scenarios.

The Facilities will be operated and maintained on a back-to-back basis with 2 people per position (1 off / 1 on)
rotating through the life of the Project. The rotation duration for each position is expected to be between 2 to 4
weeks.

The Project's operations and maintenance approach will also account for the cold climate and seasonal operating
conditions of Cook Inlet, including cold weather operations, seasonal ice presence, and reduced daylight and
weather-related access limitations, which will be incorporated into operational planning and scheduling.

Final operating arrangements, including staffing, shift structure, and organizational interfaces, will be defined
during later project stages and reflected in the applicable operating manuals and procedures.

1.6.2    MAINTENANCE
The Project's maintenance philosophy is based on a combination of preventive maintenance, condition-based
monitoring, and periodic inspection and testing. Maintenance activities will be planned to minimize disruption
to gas supply, with scheduled maintenance coordinated where practicable with LNG delivery cycles, seasonal
demand patterns, and regulatory requirements.

Major systems will be designed to allow maintenance in place to the greatest extent practicable. An inspection
and integrity management approach will be applied to all critical systems, including the non-jurisdictional LNG
storage, regasification, and gas transfer systems associated with the FSRU, as well as the mooring and berthing
system, and the jurisdictional Osprey platform and downstream pipeline infrastructure. Inspection intervals and
methods will be consistent with applicable codes, standards, and class requirements, and will be refined as
operating experience is gained.

Maintenance of the converted pipeline system will be governed by 49 C.F.R. Part 192, Subpart M, requiring
written maintenance procedures under 49 C.F.R. § 192.605, regular inspection of pipeline components including
valves and fittings, prompt repair of identified deficiencies or anomalies, and recordkeeping to demonstrate
regulatory compliance. Personnel conducting maintenance activities will be required to be qualified and trained
consistent with operator qualification standards under Subpart N.

Existing subsea and onshore pipelines retained for the Project are subject to inline inspection, pressure testing,
and flow assurance analysis prior to being placed into gas service. Results of these assessments will govern the
final scope of any pipeline modifications required.

The Class I Underground Injection Control (UIC) disposal wells serving the Project (one on the Osprey Platform
and one at WMR) are essential to maintaining zero-discharge regulatory status for the platform and camp
wastewater streams, respectively, and will be maintained in good working order for as long as their associated
facilities remain in service. Neither well is included within the scope of well plugging and abandonment
associated with the cessation of prior oil production operations. CILNG will become the Operator of Record for
both Class I injection wells and continue to maintain them per EPA requirements.

All major Project systems will be designed for a minimum service life of at least 20 years with inspection,
maintenance, and integrity management programs structured to support this design life.

1.11 CUMULATIVE IMPACTS AND INDIRECT EFFECTS
Under 40 C.F.R. § 1508.7, a cumulative impact is defined as “the impact on the environment which results from
the incremental impact of the action when added to other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions,
regardless of what agency (Federal or non-Federal) or person undertakes such other actions. Cumulative impacts
can result from individually minor but collectively significant actions taking place over a period of time.”
Similarly, FERC guidance for preparation of environmental reports defines a reasonably foreseeable action as
one with a realistic probability of occurring.

Cumulative impacts may occur when the environmental effects of the Project are combined with those of other
projects in the same geographic area or resource setting. While the incremental impacts of any one project may
be minor, when considered together they may become significant. Except for the mooring anchor placement area
located adjacent to the Osprey platform, the CILNG Project’s construction and operations are confined to the
existing Project site, which has supported oil and gas operations for more than 40 years. Ground disturbance
onshore will be limited to minor subsurface work for piping, electrical tie-ins, and equipment installation, all of
which will occur within previously developed industrial land and existing easements. Installation of the mooring
anchors will occur within a gross area of roughly 222 acres, though each mooring anchor itself will impact only

2.1     PROJECT DESCRIPTION
Natural gas serves as a critical energy source for Southcentral Alaska. This has been true since the 1950’s, when
low-cost gas was available as a by-product of oil produced in the Cook Inlet. Natural gas is demanded by
regional utilities for both power generation and consumer heating service, by industrial users such as the
Port of Alaska and a regional refinery, and by commercial facilities (businesses, government, and non-
governmental users). Alaska Department of Natural Resources (ADNR) estimates1 that from 2016 to 2021,
gas demand averaged 68 billion cubic feet (Bcf) per year and that this demand was roughly comprised of
21% commercial, 35% electricity, 28% residential, and 15% for oil and gas operations.
In early 2022, Cook Inlet producers announced they would no longer be able to support long-term supply
contracts as remaining reserves were insufficient. Shortly thereafter, regional utilities and the State of Alaska
formed a working group to address the issue and studies determined that significant supply shortfalls could begin
as early as 2029 and certainly by 2031 as shown in [1]. To address the significant gas supply shortfall projected
for southcentral Alaska as early as 2029, the Cook Inlet LNG Project (“Project”) seeks to develop a Floating
Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU)-based gas receiving terminal that maximizes the use of existing oil and gas
production infrastructure (platform, pipelines and facilities) both onshore and offshore of the West Foreland
in Cook Inlet. (Figure 1.) As planned, the Project contemplates delivering between 20 and 40 Bcf/year of gas to
market customers 1 and will consist of the following FERC-jurisdictional components situated on a total of
507.13 gross acres of State lands, private lands and land that will be owned by the Project:
      a) a converted oil & gas production platform (Osprey Platform) located on approximately 0.4 acres of
         State of Alaska submerged lands in State waters approximately 1.8-miles offshore of West Foreland
         that will receive regasified liquified natural gas (LNG) (vaporous gas) from an FSRU equipped with
         a high-pressure gas transfer system;
      b) a Buoy Spread Mooring System composed of 20 drag embedment anchors each measuring 7m x
         7.5m (575 sq ft), spread out over a gross area of approximately 214 acres of State of Alaska
         submerged lands in State waters;
      c) existing subsea and onshore pipelines situated on uplands within both State of Alaska and private
         pipeline easements ranging in width from 20-feet to 600-feet (totaling 179.4 gross acres) and
         connecting the Osprey Platform (Mile 0) to an onshore metering station (Mile 11) at the termination
         of the Project where the gas will be delivered into the regional gas pipeline system. Pipeline
         easements run immediately adjacent to the non-public gravel access road, along its west side.
         Existing pipelines, which have been used to transport oil (8-inch steel), natural gas (6-inch steel) and
         produced water (8-inch steel and Flex-Steel), will be inspected and tested. Three discrete segments
         between KPF and MOS, totaling approximately 7.8 miles in cumulative total length, will be replaced
         or upgraded as required to address integrity or throughput issues. This equates to approximately
         46.6 gross acres of disturbance within the existing pipeline right-of-way. All pipelines will be
         converted to natural gas transmission service through the Conversion of Service procedures and
         process stipulated by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) under
         49 CFR Part 192. All pipeline conversion, replacement, and testing will take place within existing
         pipeline easements and construction rights-of-way located on uplands. No wetlands or new,

(approximately 11.3 pipeline miles from Osprey Platform) will mark the terminus of the Project and Project
ownership of the pipeline.
The Project is designed to operate safely in the unique environmental conditions of Cook Inlet. Similar designs
have been proven and are operating safely and successfully in other demanding locations worldwide. All
aspects of the Cook Inlet LNG Project represent industry standard applications and reflect best practices of

2.2       GROUNDWATER RESOURCES
This section describes the existing groundwater resources in the Project area, including groundwater use and

the Project and methods to avoid, minimize, and mitigate those potential impacts.
2.2.1     REGIONAL HYDROGEOLOGY
The land immediately west of Trading Bay lies within the Cook Inlet Lowlands, one of the wettest and most
hydrologically complex landscapes in southcentral Alaska (see Figure 2). Regional hydrology is controlled by
an interaction of tides, glacial rivers, wetlands, shallow groundwater, and very low topographic relief.
The landscape consists primarily of both freshwater and tidal marshes, mudflats, peatlands, streams, rivers, and
numerous lakes and ponds. Much of the terrain has slopes of 1% or less, resulting in very slow water movement
across the landscape [3].
The area west of Trading Bay is drained by several west Cook Inlet rivers, including:
      •   McArthur River
      •   Kustatan River
      •   Big River
These rivers generally originate in the Alaska Range foothills and flow eastward into Cook Inlet through
extremely broad wetland complexes. Numerous smaller unnamed sloughs and drainage channels interconnect
these rivers before reaching the coast [3].
The West Foreland of Cook Inlet on which the Project resides, marks the southern boundary of Trading Bay
where the McArthur River flats form an expansive network of freshwater marshes landward of a tidal wetland
fringe. Just to the south and west lies the Kustatan River floodplain which is almost entirely characterized as a
low-lying wetlands system. The prominent geographical feature that is the eastern-most point of the West
Foreland is a coastal bluff of glacial origin representing part of a major glacial moraine that was built during the
late Pleistocene epoch as massive glaciers in the Cook Inlet basin repeatedly advanced and retreated.

2.2.2   GROUNDWATER QUALITY AND USE
Groundwater resources and quality in the Cook Inlet region were assessed by reviewing an in-depth study
conducted by US Geological Survey and reviewed by Glass [4]. Water quality is generally within drinking water
standards established by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; however, naturally occurring arsenic, iron,
and manganese exceeded the maximum contaminant levels in some of the study’s samples.
Groundwater is generally shallow, and streams are recharged by groundwater seepage during low water periods.
Deeper in the geologic section, the Beluga and Sterling Formations have water sources separate from the more
acidic shallow groundwater in the peatlands. Elevated levels of arsenic, iron, and manganese are common
throughout the region. In 1999, arsenic levels up to 29 micrograms per liter were found in Cook Inlet
groundwater, which exceeds the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s maximum contaminant level of 10
micrograms per liter. The 2001 Glass [4] review of U.S. Geological Survey groundwater samples collected in
the Cook Inlet Basin showed that nearly a third of the samples had arsenic concentrations of 10 micrograms per
liter or greater, and 4 percent had arsenic levels greater than 50 micrograms per liter. The potential health effects
from long-term exposure to arsenic include skin damage, problems with the circulatory system, and increased
cancer risk [5].
2.2.3   PUBLIC AND PRIVATE WATER SUPPLY WELLS AND SPRINGS
There are five water supply wells within the area of Project facilities that currently supply existing production
facilities and camps (see Figures 3 and 4). Two water supply wells, a 1974-drilled un-numbered UNOCAL well,
and the LAS 30829 well are located approximately 0.2 miles west of the airstrip at the Trading Bay Production
Facility and will not be used or impacted by the Project. In addition to these wells, there is one well LAS 21452
approximately 3.5 miles south of the Trading Bay Production Facility and outside of the Project area. The LAS
23583 and LAS 26422 wells supply the KPF as needed.

minimized through the use of BMPs as outlined in FERC’s (Construction Methods....). No groundwater
withdrawals will be required for the construction of the Project. Further, the groundwater withdrawals for the
operation of the existing facilities will not increase but will actually decrease due to the termination of oil
production activities and the reduced manpower requirements of the Project and related decrease in use of camp
facilities. Therefore, the Project will not result in a lowering of the local groundwater table.
The Project will maintain a Construction Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure (SPCC) Plan and a
Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) per ADEC and EPA requirements which will include provisions
to prevent unforeseen impacts on groundwater resources and provide guidance for responding to and addressing
any accidental releases properly during construction and operation of the Project. In addition, the Project will
adhere to all applicable federal and state water quality and stormwater standards (e.g., Clean Water Act, Sections
401, 402, and 404, the Safe Drinking Water Act, National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Stormwater
Program) to prevent adverse effects on the quality of groundwater resources. All Project construction will take
place within existing and previously disturbed pipeline easements and construction rights-of-way, estimated to
impact a total of approximately 44 gross acres.
2.2.5   HYDROSTATIC TESTING
Hydrostatic testing of existing and any new pipeline segments will be required for the Project as a part of the
PHMSA Conversion of Service process under 49 CFR Part 192. Based upon past operational experience at the
Project location, approximately 3000 barrels of testing fluid was required for testing the entire length of pipeline
from Osprey Platform to MOS. All fluid for hydrostatic testing will be sourced from an existing, lined water
storage area near WMR. If other makeup water were to be required, surface water from a nearby non-perennial
pond could be authorized by ADNR under a Temporary Water Use Authorization. All hydrostatic test water will
recycled and reused in the process to the maximum extent possible. Upon completion of testing, hydrostatic
testing fluids will be disposed of through an existing EPA Class I non-hazardous disposal well located at WMR
which the Project will own and operate. The use of off-site water sources is not anticipated for the Project.
2.3     SURFACE WATER RESOURCES
The National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) was reviewed to identify mapped rivers, streams, and ponds[6] within
and/or adjacent to the Project area. The NHD is a database used to map, navigate, and analyze the surface water
drainage network of the US.
The NHD dataset revealed there are three identified surface water resources in the vicinity of, but not within, the
proposed Project area – The McArthur River and the Kustatan River, and the Big River. The McArthur River
lies approximately 7 miles directly north of the Trading Bay Production Facility, the Kustatan River flows into
Cook Inlet approximately 4.5 miles directly southwest of Kustatan Production Facilities, approximately 4.5
miles from the Osprey Platform, and the Big River flows into Cook Inlet approximately 10 miles west of KPF
(see Figure 4.)
The Project is not expected to impact any of these surface water resources.

3.    RESOURCE REPORT 3 – FISH, WILDLIFE, AND VEGETATION
3.1     INTRODUCTION
Natural gas serves as a critical energy source for Southcentral Alaska. This has been true since the 1950’s, when
low-cost gas was available as a by-product of oil produced in the Cook Inlet. Natural gas is demanded by
regional utilities for both power generation and consumer heating service, by industrial users such as the
Port of Alaska and a regional refinery, and by commercial facilities (businesses, government, and non-
governmental users). Alaska Department of Natural Resources (ADNR) estimates1 that from 2016 to 2021,
gas demand averaged 68 billion cubic feet (Bcf) per year and that this demand was roughly comprised of
21% commercial, 35% electricity, 28% residential, and 15% for oil and gas operations.
In early 2022, Cook Inlet producers announced they would no longer be able to support long-term supply
contracts as remaining reserves were insufficient. Shortly thereafter, regional utilities and the State of Alaska
formed a working group to address the issue and studies determined that significant supply shortfalls could begin
as early as 2029 and certainly by 2031 as shown in [1]. To address the significant gas supply shortfall projected
for southcentral Alaska as early as 2029, the Cook Inlet LNG Project (“Project”) seeks to develop a Floating
Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU)-based gas receiving terminal that maximizes the use of existing oil and gas
production infrastructure (platform, pipelines and facilities) both onshore and offshore of the West Foreland
in Cook Inlet. (Figure 1.) As planned, the Project contemplates delivering between 20 and 40 Bcf/year of gas to
market customers1 and will consist of the following FERC-jurisdictional components situated on a total of 507.13
gross acres of State lands, private lands and land that will be owned by the Project:
      a) a converted oil & gas production platform (Osprey Platform) located on approximately 0.4 acres of
         State of Alaska submerged lands in State waters approximately 1.8-miles offshore of West Foreland
         that will receive regasified liquified natural gas (LNG) (vaporous gas) from an FSRU equipped with
         a high-pressure gas transfer system;
      b) a Buoy Spread Mooring System composed of 20 drag embedment anchors each measuring 7m x
         7.5m (575 sq ft), spread out over a gross area of approximately 214 acres of State of Alaska
         submerged lands in State waters;
      c) existing subsea and onshore pipelines situated on uplands within both State of Alaska and private
         pipeline easements ranging in width from 20-feet to 600-feet (totaling 179.4 gross acres) and
         connecting the Osprey Platform (Mile 0) to an onshore metering station (Mile 11) at the termination
         of the Project where the gas will be delivered into the regional gas pipeline system. Pipeline
         easements run immediately adjacent to the non-public gravel access road, along its west side.
         Existing pipelines, which have been used to transport oil (8-inch steel), natural gas (6-inch steel) and
         produced water (8-inch steel and Flex-Steel), will be inspected and tested. Three discrete segments
         between KPF and MOS, totaling approximately 7.8 miles in cumulative total length, will be replaced
         or upgraded as required to address integrity or throughput issues. This equates to approximately
         46.6 gross acres of disturbance within the existing pipeline right-of-way. All pipelines will be
         converted to natural gas transmission service through the Conversion of Service procedures and
         process stipulated by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) under
         49 CFR Part 192. All pipeline conversion, replacement, and testing will take place within existing
         pipeline easements and construction rights-of-way located on uplands. No wetlands or new,

    e) related existing onshore auxiliary support facilities including an operations center, man camp

       facility operators under a private surface use easement. These facilities are not open to the public and

       within previously disturbed upland areas and are authorized under existing surface land use
       easements on private land or are on land that will be owned by the Project. Auxiliary facilities are
       distributed along the pipeline corridor at Mile 4 (KPF), Mile 8.5 (WMR) and Mile 11.3 (MOS) and
       encompass a total of approximately 53.5 gross acres.
The Project utilizes an FSRU which is a non-jurisdictional project component not subject to FERC’s
authorization, siting approval, or environmental oversight under the Natural Gas Act. The jurisdictional
authority for the FSRU, its offshore siting and the STS transfer of LNG to the FSRU is the U. S. Coast Guard.
Construction of the Project will enable the long-term (not permanently fixed) mooring of a modern 145,000 to
165,000 cubic meter capacity FSRU approximately 120 meters south-southeast of the Osprey Platform for the
purpose of transferring vaporous natural gas to shore through existing subsea pipelines discussed above which
are located within a 600-foot-wide pipeline easement issued and administered by the State of Alaska. Roughly
every 30 to 45 days, LNG will be transferred via industry standard ship-to-ship (STS) transfer operations from
visiting LNG carriers to the FSRU. LNG will be regasified on the FSRU and transferred through the FSRU’s
high-pressure flexible, gas transfer lines suspended above the waters of Cook Inlet and running from the FSRU
to the platform. From that point, gas will travel from the Osprey Platform through existing subsea and onshore
pipelines (2 each 8-inch diameter pipeline and one 6-inch diameter pipeline) owned by the Project. Gas will
travel to a pipe manifold and metering station at the end of the pipeline corridor where gas from the three
pipelines will be joined into one stream in a 12-inch diameter segment of upgraded pipe and finally pass through
the custody transfer meter prior to entering the regional gas pipeline system. The short, upgraded segment of
12-inch pipeline will be approximately 1050 feet long and replace an existing 6-inch diameter segment which
has insufficient capacity for the Project’s volumes. Two other segments of existing 8-inch pipeline running
between KPF and MOS will require replacement due to integrity issues and all related pipeline replacement
work will take place within the existing and previously disturbed easements and construction rights-of-way
described above. Gas entry into the regional pipeline network near the existing Trading Bay Production facilities
(approximately 11.3 pipeline miles from Osprey Platform) will mark the terminus of the Project and Project
ownership of the pipeline.
The Project is designed to operate safely in the unique environmental conditions of Cook Inlet. Similar designs
have been proven and are operating safely and successfully in other demanding locations worldwide. All

3.1.1   PURPOSE OF RESOURCE REPORT
Resource Report 3 evaluates existing fish, wildlife, and vegetation resources within the Project Area and assesses
potential impacts resulting from project operation and maintenance. The report identifies sensitive habitats,
fisheries, wetlands, vegetation communities, and protected species; evaluates potential effects on biodiversity
and ecological resources; and outlines proposed mitigation, protection, and restoration measures to minimize
environmental impacts and support regulatory compliance.
3.1.2   EFFECT DETERMINATION TERMINOLOGY
The following definitions were used when assessing the duration, significance, and outcome of potential effects
related to the Project:
    •   Duration
           o   Temporary effects are those that could occur only during a specific phase of the Project, such as
               during construction or installation activities.
           o   Short-term effects could continue up to five years.
           o   Long-term effects are those that would require more than five years to recover.
           o   Permanent effects could occur as a result of any activity that modified a resource to the extent
               that it would not return to preconstruction conditions during the 30-year life of the Project.
    •   Significance
           o   Minor effects are those that could be perceptible but are of very low intensity and may be too
               small to measure.
           o   Significant effects are those that, in their context, and due to their intensity, have the potential to
               result in a substantial adverse change in the physical, biological, or human environment.
    •   Outcome
           o   A positive effect may cause positive outcomes to the natural or human environment.
           o   An adverse effect may cause unfavorable or undesirable outcomes to the natural or human
               environment.
           o   Direct effects are “caused by the action and occur at the same time and place” (40 C.F.R. 1508.8).
           o   Indirect effects are “caused by an action and are later in time or farther removed in distance but
               are still reasonably foreseeable. Indirect impacts may include growth inducing effects and other
               effects related to induced changes in the pattern of land use, population density or growth rate,
               and related effects on air and water and other natural systems, including ecosystems” (40 C.F.R.
               1508.8). Indirect impacts are caused by the Project, but do not occur at the same time or place as
               the direct impacts.

3.2   FISHERIES AND OTHER AQUATIC RESOURCES
Fisheries and aquatic resources in Cook Inlet support subsistence, commercial, sport, and personal use harvest,
as well as salmon enhancement activities conducted through regional hatchery programs. Commercial fisheries
in the region occur primarily in marine and estuarine waters, while sport, subsistence and personal use fisheries
take place in both freshwater and marine environments as described in [3].
Commercial fisheries in Cook Inlet target Pacific salmon, halibut, groundfish, smelt, and herring. Groundfish
species, primarily Pacific cod and sablefish, are harvested using pots and jigs, and longline gear, while
commercial halibut are taken by longline. The Upper Cook Inlet commercial salmon fishery relies on set and
drift gillnet gear. This fishery captures all five species of Pacific salmon migrating through Upper Cook Inlet,
with many stocks originating from the Kenai and Susitna Rivers as described in [3].
Sport fishing is an important industry in Cook Inlet, with anglers targeting salmon, halibut, rockfish, and Pacific
cod in marine areas, and primarily salmon in freshwater systems as described in [4]. Within Upper Cook Inlet,
major river systems such as the Kenai and Susitna Rivers support much of the region’s freshwater salmon sport
harvest, while the Kustatan River is the most productive sport fishery closest to the Project area.
Personal use fisheries are also a major component of the fisheries and aquatic resources in Cook Inlet. The most
substantial personal use fisheries in the Upper Cook Inlet occur in the Kenai and Kasilof Rivers, where the
seasonal dipnet season attracts substantial participation from Alaska residents as described in [5].

The entirety of the Project area is located in the Cook Inlet Basin Ecoregion. Around 26 resident and

3.2.1.1.1   Sockeye Salmon
Sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka) are an important species that provide a valuable resource for commercial,
sport, and subsistence fisheries throughout Cook Inlet. The major runs in this region are found in the Kenai and
Susitna tributaries, with a relatively small population being found in the nearby Kustatan River. Sockeye salmon
typically live one to three years in freshwater systems as juveniles, before migrating to marine systems as
“smolts” (ADF&G 2026d). In systems without lakes, many juveniles travel to the ocean not long after emerging
from the gravel. As the sockeyes return to their spawning ground at the end of their life-cycle, the females
typically deposit 2,000 to 4,500 eggs as described in [6]. In Upper Cook Inlet waters, adult sockeyes are present
from June to October. In 2024, the drift gillnet fishery in the Upper Cook Inlet recorded in [8] a peak day of
harvest on July 18, with 264,034 sockeyes harvested.

3.2.1.1.2   Chinook Salmon
Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), the largest of all Pacific salmon, spawn in rivers throughout the
region. Tributaries surrounding the Susitna, Kenai, and Kasilof have historically had the largest runs of Chinooks
in the region, with nearby rivers like the Kustatan and Big River having a relatively small Chinook run. This
species has historically provided a subsistence, commercial and sport resource for the Cook Inlet area, but recent
conservation concerns have significantly affected management practices. As described in [7], Chinook Salmon
hatch in fresh water and typically rear in main-channel river areas for 1 year. Chinooks then turn into smolt the
following spring and migrate to saltwater estuaries, where they then spend 1-5 years feeding in the ocean. Since
the sexual maturity in Chinook salmon ranges from 2-7 years, there can be a vast difference in sizes of fish
during a particular spawning run. Cook Inlet rivers typically receive Chinook salmon runs from May through
July, with some rivers, such as the Kenai, experiencing distinct early- and late-run populations.

3.2.1.1.3   Coho Salmon
Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) occur in the majority of river systems within Cook Inlet, contributing to
a productive commercial and sport fishing industry in the region. Located 3 miles west of the FSRU/Platform
lies the Kustatan River, which supports a large Coho salmon run. This sport fishery is often seen as one of the
strongest on the west side of Cook Inlet, attracting sport fishermen across the state. Other major producers of
Coho salmon in Cook Inlet include the Kenai and Susitna Rivers. As described in [7], Coho salmon typically
hatch in early spring, with the embryos remaining in the gravel until they emerge in May or June. As juveniles,
Cohos spend one to three winters in streams or up to five winters in lakes before traveling to the sea as smolt.
Most Coho salmon spend 18 months at sea before returning to their original spawning grounds as adults. At the
spawning grounds, female Cohos deposit 2,400 to 4,500 eggs.

3.2.1.1.4   Pink Salmon
Pink salmon (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha) are the smallest of the pacific salmon, weighing on average between
3.5 and 5 pounds according to [7]. Found in virtually every river and stream in Cook Inlet, Pink salmon contribute
moderately to the commercial and sport fishing industries. In the Upper Cook Inlet, these salmon are commonly
incidentally harvested when targeting other species, such as Sockeye or Coho. As described in [4], Pink salmon
are more commonly targeted for commercial fisheries in the Lower Cook Inlet, where purse seine operations
harvest fish for the canning industry. Pink salmon complete their life cycle in 2 years, which results in 2 distinct
odd-year and even-year populations. On the even years, large runs of Pinks are abundant, while the odd years
have substantially smaller runs of fish. As outlined in [7], when Pink salmon emerge from the gravel beds as fry,
they immediately migrate to the ocean. After feeding in the ocean for 18 months, mature Pink salmon return to
their spawning grounds between late June and mid-October.

3.2.1.1.5   Chum Salmon

3.2.2.1    GULF OF ALASKA GROUNDFISH EFH
The Gulf of Alaska Groundfish Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) includes nearshore waters, the continental shelf,
slope, and deep offshore areas that support spawning, feeding, growth, and shelter for federally managed
groundfish species. These habitats range from kelp forests and rocky reefs to sandy, muddy, and gravel seafloor
and submarine canyons. Ocean productivity from currents, freshwater input, and seasonal upwelling supports
the food web that sustains these fish populations. Species include Alaska Pollock, Pacific and Black Cod, all
Rockfish species, flatfish such as Flounder, Halibut, Soles, and Skate species.
3.2.2.2    PACIFIC SALMON EFH
Alaska Pacific Salmon Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) includes freshwater spawning and rearing habitats, estuarine
transition zones, nearshore coastal waters, and offshore marine feeding areas that are necessary to support all
life stages of Pacific salmon. These interconnected habitats provide critical functions such as egg incubation in
stream gravels, juvenile rearing and refuge in freshwater and estuarine environments, migratory corridors
between freshwater and marine systems, and adult feeding areas in offshore waters. Maintenance of habitat
connectivity, water quality, natural flow regimes, and intact riparian and nearshore ecosystems is essential to
sustaining salmon populations and associated commercial, recreational, and subsistence fisheries. The EFH is
critical for Chinook, Coho, Chum, Sockeye, and Pink salmon.
3.2.2.3    SCALLOP EFH
Cook Inlet Weathervane Scallop Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) includes offshore benthic habitats on the
continental shelf and upper slope that support scallop spawning, larval settlement, growth, and adult feeding.

3.2.3   COMMERCIAL AND RECREATIONAL FISHERIES
Cook Inlet fishing activity is centered primarily on Pacific salmon, but also includes halibut, groundfish, and
other marine species. These fisheries are among the most intensively managed in Alaska due to overlapping user
groups, variable salmon returns, and the inlet’s proximity to major population centers.
Commercial fishing in Cook Inlet is dominated by salmon harvests, with sockeye salmon representing the largest
portion of the catch, followed by coho, chinook, chum, and pink salmon. Commercial salmon fishing occurs
primarily through drift gillnet and set gillnet operations, with gear types and fishing areas regulated by season
and location. The commercial fishery provides significant economic benefits to communities on the Kenai
Peninsula and in lower Cook Inlet, supporting fishermen, processors, tenders, and related businesses. In addition
to salmon, commercial harvests in parts of Cook Inlet and adjacent waters include halibut, herring, groundfish,
and shellfish, though these fisheries are generally smaller in scale than salmon.
Management of commercial fishing in Cook Inlet has evolved in recent years. As of May 2024, NOAA Fisheries
assumed management authority for salmon fishing in the Cook Inlet EEZ, which includes federal waters beyond
three nautical miles offshore. This shift introduced new federal permitting, reporting, and regulatory
requirements, particularly affecting commercial drift gillnet operations and seafood processors operating in those
waters. State management by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game continues within state waters, creating
a shared management framework across jurisdictions.
The most recent regulatory change that will change the landscape of the commercial fishing industry in Cook
Inlet will take effect at the start of the 2026 season. The Alaska Board of Fisheries chose to adopt and revise
Proposal 186, which limits where drift fleets in the Upper Cook Inlet can harvest their catch. This regulation
change found in [11] excludes the fleet from harvesting in Drift Gillnet Area 1 and 2, limiting fishing to Areas
2 and 3. While the harvest area becomes reduced with the new regulations, the fleet could gain up to eight
additional fishing hours per week compared to the existing rules according to [11]. The change is in response to
declined coho salmon escapements in the Upper Cook Inlet, particularly salmon bound for the Deshka and Little
Susitna Rivers. Many commercial fishermen in Upper Cook Inlet oppose this new regulation, citing that the new
restrictions will significantly limit harvest opportunities for members of the fleet.
Recreational fishing is also a major component of Cook Inlet’s fishing landscape and is a key driver of tourism
in Southcentral Alaska. Sport anglers target salmon in both freshwater and marine environments. Chinook and
sockeye salmon are particularly prized, though anglers pursue all five salmon species depending on the season.
Marine recreational fishing in Cook Inlet and nearby waters also targets halibut, rockfish, and cod. Recreational
salmon fishing in federal waters of Cook Inlet is allowed under federal regulations, while anglers must comply
with state rules when landing fish in Alaska.
Subsistence and personal use fishing play an essential role in Cook Inlet communities, especially for Alaska
Native Villages and rural residents. Subsistence fisheries support food security, cultural practices, and
intergenerational knowledge, with salmon forming the backbone of these harvests. Personal use fisheries, which
are distinct from both subsistence and sport fishing, allow Alaska residents to harvest salmon for household
consumption and have grown significantly in participation in recent decades. In some years, personal use
harvests account for a substantial share of the total noncommercial salmon take in the region.

3.2.4     AQUATIC NUISANCE AND NONINDIGENOUS ANIMALS
Nonindigenous or invasive species can disrupt ecological systems by altering natural balances and suppressing
native species. They can also negatively affect commercial industries, as well as subsistence and recreational
fisheries. To address these threats and limit their impact on Alaska’s ecosystems, ADF&G developed [12], the
Aquatic Nuisance Species (ANS) Management Plan, which targets nonindigenous species that have already
entered, or could potentially enter Alaskan waters. Originally created in 2002, [12] was designed to promote
coordination both within ADF&G divisions and among other agencies for the prevention, early detection, and
management of invasive species. Adoption of the ANS plan also enabled the State of Alaska to receive limited
federal funding through the Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force (ANSTF), a federal intergovernmental body,
co-chaired by the USFWS and NOAA, that coordinates national efforts to prevent, detect, and control invasive
aquatic species.
3.2.4.1     AQUATIC NUISANCE SPECIES (ANS)
There is one aquatic nuisance species in Cook Inlet that ADF&G has identified with the potential to impact the
waters around Cook Inlet as a High Priority Threat, meaning it poses a significant risk to Alaskan ecosystems
and require immediate or ongoing management to minimize its effect.
In addition to the ANS plan, the Northen Pike waters catalog from ADF&G’s Alaska Fish Resource Monitor
showed several lakes and streams in Upper Cook Inlet that have confirmed infestations of Northern Pike.
3.2.4.1.1    Northern Pike
Northern Pike (Esox lucius) are native to Interior Alaska but have been illegally introduced into Southcentral
Alaska on numerous occasions, where they pose significant threats to native fish populations. Their coloration
ranges from light to dark green, and they have elongated bodies with a flat, duck-bill like snout as described in
[13]. Pike overwinter in large, slow-moving rivers and reach sexual maturity between four and six years of age.
Spawning occurs in the spring as ice melts, with females laying eggs in grassy shorelines, sloughs, or slow-
moving streams, where incubation lasts about 30 days. During the summer months, pike feed in warm, shallow
waters. According to [13], Northen pike can live over 20 years.
Initially introduced in Southcentral Alaska by private landowners in the 1950s, Northern pike has since spread
to connected lakes and streams throughout the region as described in [14]. Recent studies have revealed that
Northern pike can use the estuarine and brackish waters of the Upper Cook Inlet as a travel corridor to colonize
lakes and streams that are isolated from pike infested waters. Pike are tolerant of short-term exposure to brackish
water, and seasonal freshwater pulses into Cook Inlet reduces salinity enough to facilitate these movements.
Several freshwater drainages near the Village of Tyonek (approximately 30 miles east of the FSRU/Platform)
have had confirmed Northern pike infestations. According to [14], continued early-detection surveys for
Northern pike in West Cook Inlet are essential to enable timely management actions, including suppression or
eradication where feasible, in order to prevent secondary infestations and protect important native fish
populations and their habitats.

3.3.1     MARINE MAMMALS
The Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) prohibits take of marine mammals without authorization
from NMFS or USFWS. As defined in [15], "take" under the MMPA means “to hunt harass, capture, or
kill” any marine mammal or attempt to do so. NMFS and USFWS are given authority to implement the
MMPA.
In the Project area, USFWS is responsible for the conservation and management of northern sea otters, and
most bird species and NMFS is responsible for management of seals, sea lions, whales, dolphins, and
porpoises.
Marine mammals potentially occurring in the Project area are listed in Table 2. ESA-listed marine mammals
are further discussed in Section 3.4.
3.3.1.1    HARBOR PORPOISE
As described in [6], harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) are small, robust marine mammals with a short
blunt beak, a triangular dorsal fin, and dark gray backs that fade to lighter gray on the sides, with white
bellies and throats and a dark chin patch. Females are slightly larger than males.
They primarily eat schooling fish such as herring and mackerel, and occasionally squid and octopus. Harbor
porpoises are shy animals, usually seen alone or in small groups, and unlike many dolphins, they avoid
boats and surface quietly by rolling and arching their backs without splashing. They live in northern
temperate, subarctic, and Arctic waters, commonly inhabiting shallow coastal areas such as bays, estuaries,
and fjords across the North Atlantic and North Pacific Oceans according to [6].
As shown in [16], the most current stock assessment (2020) states that the abundance estimate for the Gulf
of Alaska stock is unknown because the existing estimate is more than 8 years old and so the PBR level is
considered undetermined.
Harbor porpoises are likely to occur near the Osprey Platform in Upper Cook Inlet.
3.3.1.2    HARBOR SEAL
Harbor seals (Phoca vitulina) are “true seals”, meaning they have short flippers, no external ear flaps, and
move on land with a caterpillar-like motion. They can grow up to 6 feet long and weigh as much as 285
pounds, with fur patterns that range from light with dark spots to dark with light rings. Harbor seals rest on
rocks, beaches, or ice to molt, give birth, and avoid predators, and their pups can swim and dive shortly
after birth. They live along temperate northern coastlines and feed mainly on fish, shellfish, and crustaceans,
diving both shallow and deep to hunt according to [6].
Harbor seals in Alaskan waters are designated as 12 separate stocks. Of these stocks, harbor seals in the
Cook Inlet Shelikof stock are likely to occur within the Project area in Upper Cook Inlet. The most current
stock assessment (2011) estimated that the Cook Inlet Shelikof stock was comprised of 22,900 seals and is
considered stable as described in [17].
3.3.2     ALASKA WILDLIFE TERRESTRIAL HABITATS
The Cook Inlet ecoregion of southcentral Alaska supports a diverse mix of terrestrial habitats shaped by
glaciation, coastal processes, and a transition from maritime to interior climates. Major habitat types include
boreal forests, wetlands, river corridors, alpine and subalpine tundra, coastal marshes, and glacial outwash
plains. Lowland areas around the inlet are dominated by spruce–hardwood forests of white spruce, paper
birch, and aspen, with black spruce and muskeg in poorly drained soils. These forests provide important
habitat for moose, black and brown bears, wolves, lynx, snowshoe hares, and a wide variety of resident and
migratory songbirds and raptors.

Extensive wetland systems occur along the Susitna, Matanuska, and Kenai lowlands and in the upper inlet,
including bogs, fens, and freshwater marshes that support waterfowl, shorebirds, and furbearers such as
beaver and muskrat. River corridors and riparian zones are highly productive, with dense willow and alder
thickets that provide key foraging and movement habitat for moose and nesting areas for birds. Along the
western and upper margins of Cook Inlet, broad tidal flats transition into coastal marshes and sedge
meadows, which are especially important for migratory birds and seasonal wildlife use.
Moving away from the lowlands, upland and mountainous areas on both the west side (Alaska Range
foothills) and east side (Chugach and Kenai mountains) shift into subalpine shrublands and alpine tundra.
These habitats support species such as caribou, wolverine, ptarmigan, and ground-nesting birds.
Disturbance-driven habitats, including areas affected by wildfire, flooding, and glacial retreat, create a
mosaic of early successional vegetation that benefits browsing species and many bird species. Overall, the
Cook Inlet terrestrial landscape is a patchwork of forest, wetland, and alpine systems that provide critical
year-round habitat for large mammals, migratory birds, and resident wildlife.
The two major Game Management Units encompassing the Cook Inlet ecoregion are units 15 and 16.
Alaska Game Management Unit 15 (GMU 15) covers the Kenai Peninsula in southcentral Alaska and
includes all lands south of Turnagain Arm and east of Cook Inlet. The unit extends from the western
shoreline along Cook Inlet across the interior of the peninsula. It encompasses a mix of lowland basins,
large river systems, and mountainous terrain, and is one of the most accessible and heavily used wildlife
management units in the state due to its proximity to Anchorage and the road system.
The western and central portions of Unit 15 are characterized by low- to moderate-elevation boreal forest,
wetlands, and river corridors associated with major drainages such as the Kenai, Kasilof, and Anchor rivers.
These areas include extensive spruce and mixed hardwood forests, muskeg, and riparian habitats. The
eastern side of the unit rises sharply into the Kenai Mountains, where terrain becomes rugged and glaciated,
with alpine and subalpine habitats, steep valleys, and numerous glaciers. Elevations increase from sea level
along Cook Inlet and the outer coast to high mountain peaks inland, creating strong ecological gradients
across the unit.
The climate varies from maritime along the southern and eastern coasts to more continental in the interior
lowlands. Coastal areas experience higher precipitation and milder temperatures, while inland portions tend
to have colder winters and warmer summers.
Alaska Game Management Unit 16 (GMU 16) is located in southcentral Alaska and lies west of Cook Inlet,
generally bounded by the inlet to the east, the Alaska Range to the north and west, and Bristol Bay drainages
to the southwest. The unit includes the lowland and upland landscapes associated with the Susitna River
basin and surrounding foothills, encompassing a large, mostly roadless area characterized by broad river
valleys, wetlands, and forested uplands. Access is limited in many areas, with most travel occurring by
boat, aircraft, or snowmachine.
The eastern portion of Unit 16 consists of low-lying terrain near Cook Inlet, with extensive wetlands,
muskeg, lakes, and slow-moving river systems. Moving inland, the landscape transitions into rolling hills
and boreal forest dominated by spruce, birch, and aspen, interspersed with riparian corridors of willow and
alder along the Susitna, Yentna, Skwentna, and Beluga river drainages. These river systems create wide
floodplains and highly productive habitat zones across much of the unit.
Toward the western and northern boundaries, elevations increase into the foothills and mountains of the
Alaska Range, where the terrain becomes more rugged and includes subalpine shrublands and alpine tundra.
Glacially influenced valleys, braided rivers, and outwash plains are common in these higher elevation areas.

restrictions and instructions that apply for each subunit, including the seasons when hunting is allowed,
what permits are required, where specific hunting is permitted, how many animals may be harvested each

The Project encompasses 2 of the 26 GMUs (15 and 16), including portions of 3 subunits (15A, 15B, 16B).
To harvest game or fur animals in Alaska, a valid state hunting or trapping license, permit, tag, or harvest
ticket is required. There are five types of non-subsistence hunts: general season, drawing, permit,
registration, and targeted. Hunting regulations, including season dates, game animals, and bag limits, vary
by GMU and hunt type. Harvest tickets are required for most big game animals and may be acquired at any
time during the year but expire at the end of the regulatory year on June 30. General season and harvest
ticket hunts do not require a permit. All other hunts require a permit and restrict harvest as outlined in [18].
Hunt types include:
    •   General Season – Hunts are open to Alaska residents and nonresidents. General season hunts are
        the least restrictive hunts and require a license, tag, or harvest ticket.
    •   Drawing Hunts – Available to both Alaska residents and nonresidents. These hunts require an
        application fee and are awarded by lottery. The application period for draw hunts is during
        November and December and must be submitted online
    •   Permit Hunts – Take place in areas where hunter demand is higher than is sustainable for game
        populations and can close early by emergency order.
    •   Registration Hunts – Boundary – specific and do not generally limit the number of permits but can
        be closed by emergency order if harvest quota is met.
    •   Targeted Hunts – Similar to registration hunts but require an application for a specific time frame.
        They are typically used to limit human-wildlife conflict, like winter moose-vehicle collisions.
        These hunts are awarded by lottery.

3.3.4.1   BLACK BEAR
Black bears (Ursus americanus) occur over most of the forested areas of the state, with an estimated
100,000 bears in Alaska. Habitats favored by black bears include riverine scrub, lowland broadleaf forest,
lowland needleleaf forest, and upland broadleaf forest. The northern limit of black bears in Alaska is the
Brooks Range – black bears are not found on the North Slope.
June through July is when mating takes place. The cubs are born in their dens following a gestation period
of about 7 months. The cubs are born blind and nearly hairless, weighing under a pound. One to four cubs
may be born, but two cubs are most common. Cubs remain with their mothers through the first winter
following birth. Black bears spend the winter months in a state of hibernation. Their body temperatures
drop, their metabolic rate is reduced, and they sleep for long periods. Bears enter this dormancy period in
the fall, after most food items become hard to find. They emerge in the spring when food is again available.
Occasionally, in the more southern ranges, bears will emerge from their dens during winter. In the northern
part of their range, black bears may be dormant for as long as seven to eight months. Females with cubs
usually emerge later than lone bears, and enter dens earlier in the fall than lone bears. Dens may be found
from sea level to alpine areas, in rock cavities, hollow trees, excavations, or even piled vegetation on the
ground.
Black bears are opportunistic, although their foraging habits follow a seasonal pattern. When emerging
from their dens in the spring, freshly sprouted vegetation is their main food item, but black bears will eat
nearly anything, including winterkill animals, human trash, and newborn moose calves. As summer
progresses, feeding shifts to salmon where available, like in the Project area. In areas where salmon is
unavailable, black bears rely on vegetation, berries, and insects as described in [22].

3.3.4.2   BROWN BEAR
Brown bears (Ursus arctos) occur throughout mainland Alaska, from the North Slope to the Alaska and
Kenai Peninsula. They also inhabit islands in Southeast Alaska, Prince William Sound, and the Kodiak
Archipelago. Brown bears are very adaptable and consume a wide variety of foods. Common foods include
salmon, berries, grasses, sedges, cow parsnip, ground squirrels, carrion, and roots. In many parts of Alaska,
brown bears are capable predators of moose and caribou, especially newborns. Bears may also be attracted
to human camps and homes by improperly stored food and garbage, as well as by domestic animals.
Cubs are born in the den during January and February. Twins are most common, but litter sizes can range
from one to four. Females and cubs emerge from dens in spring. The mating season is in the spring (May
to July). Bears enter their dens around September to late October, depending on the geographic area, and
remain there until spring. Pregnant females are usually the first to enter dens in the fall. These females, with
their newborn cubs, are the last to exit dens. Adult males, on the other hand, enter dens later and emerge
earlier than most other bears. In northern areas, bears may spend up to eight months in dens, while in areas
with relatively mild winters, such as Kodiak, some male bears stay active all winter. Bears den in a variety
of terrain ranging from pingos, streams, and lake banks at low elevations, to mountain slopes.
Bear populations in Alaska are considered healthy. Bear density within an area depends on the quality of
the habitat. In areas of low productivity, such as on Alaska’s North Slope, bear density may be as low as
one bear per 300 square miles. Where food is abundant, bear density may be as high as one bear per square
mile. In Interior Alaska, bear densities tend to be intermediate with about one bear per 15 to 25 square miles
according to [23].

3.3.4.3   MOOSE
Alaska supports about 175,000 to 200,000 moose (Alces americanus) that are widely distributed across
most of the state. Moose are especially abundant on timberline plateaus, along major rivers of Southcentral
and Interior Alaska, and on recently burned areas that have dense stands of willow, aspen, and birch shrubs.
Moose calve in the spring, with calves weaned in the fall. Breeding occurs in late September and early
October. During fall and winter, moose consume willow birch and aspen twigs. During summer, moose
feed on forbs, vegetation in shallow ponds, and the leaves of birch willow and aspen. Moose make seasonal
movements between calving, rutting, and wintering areas, traveling from a few miles to as many as 60
miles. Suitable moose habitat is characterized by mixed forest elements, dominated by white spruce, black
spruce, paper birch, quaking aspen, and balsam poplar. Shrub communities of alder and willow are most
common in riparian sites and surrounding lakes and meadows. Dwarf shrubs such as resin birch (Betula
glandulosa), Labrador tea (Ledum decumbens), crowberry (Empetrum nigrum), and blueberry (Vaccinium
uliginosum) are common in the uplands.
Before 1940, moose were uncommon in Unit 16B. Since then, habitat changes and federal predator control
allowed the population to increase. Moose populations fluctuate greatly in Unit 16B due to heavy snow
years that seem to occur once or twice every decade. Moose in this unit likely numbered more than 10,000
during the early 1980s. Before the severe winter of 1989–1990, there likely were 8,500–9,500 moose.
Following a 15–20% decline after winter 1989–1990, moose numbers in the unit continued to decline in
response to deep snow winters and increasing predation according to [24].

3.3.4.4   WOLF
Wolves (Canis lupus) occur throughout mainland Alaska, with an estimated population of 7,000 to 11,000.
Wolves are found within nearly all their historic range, except in urban areas; although, they are found on
the outskirts of Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Juneau. Wolves are social animals and usually live in packs that
include parents and pups of the year. The average pack size is six or seven animals. Pack members often
include some yearlings and other adults, and packs maintain territories. Packs of 20 to 30 wolves sometimes
occur, and these larger packs may have two or three litters of pups from more than one female. Typically,
one female wolf in a pack has a litter of about seven pups each year. Pups are born in dens. Most adult male
wolves in Interior Alaska weigh from 85 to 115 pounds; females average 10 to 15 pounds lighter and rarely
weigh more than 110 pounds. In most of mainland Alaska, moose and/or caribou are the primary prey for
wolves, with Dall sheep, squirrels, snowshoe hares, beaver, and occasionally birds and fish as supplements
in the diet. The rate at which wolves kill large mammals varies with prey availability and environmental
conditions.
Prior to the 1900s and the establishment of major human settlements in Anchorage and surrounding areas,
wolf numbers in Unit 16 fluctuated with prey densities. Since 1900 wolf populations have been heavily
influenced by various human harvest regimes ranging from predator control strategies prior to statehood
(including the use of poison, bounties, and aerial shooting) to relatively restrictive regulations including
only trapping and sport hunting.
In 2003, a wolf control implementation plan was initiated in response to declining moose numbers and a
high wolf population in 16B. Initially, the implementation of the plan included the use of snowmachines to
take wolves, but land-and-shoot wolf control began in December 2004 and was amended in February 2005
to include same day airborne shooting (SDA) of wolves by permittees. The SDA program allowed pilots to
apply for permits to harvest wolves from the air. Applications were screened by the area manager and
participation in the program was limited to approximately 30 permitted pilots. During the first year of the
program SDA teams took 91 wolves. Harvest in subsequent years from hunters, trappers, and SDA teams
reduced the population to levels near the intensive management (IM) population objective as described in
[25]. The predator control program was reauthorized for 6 years and modified to include brown bear
predation control in March 2011. In February 2015, the predator control program was again reauthorized
for 6 years and included an Operational Plan for Intensive Management of Moose. Under this plan the wolf
population objective was 35–55 wolves.

all year, staying in their nests only during severe cold spells or inclement weather. Red squirrels are solitary,
except during mating in February and March. Young are born 36 to 40 days later and remain with their
mother until the following winter. In summer, red squirrels spend most of their time cutting and storing
green spruce cones in caches. They also eat mushrooms, seeds, berries, buds, fungi, and occasionally insects
and bird eggs. Nests are either built in a hole in a tree trunk or made of tightly constructed mass of twigs,
leaves, mosses, and lichens in the densest foliage of a tree. Main predators of the red squirrel include hawks,

3.3.5.2   AMERICAN BEAVER
Beavers (Castor canadensis) are distributed over most of Alaska from near the crest of the Brooks Range
south to the middle of the Alaska Peninsula. Beavers inhabit lakes, ponds, marshes, rivers, and streams,
where they create wetland habitats that are used by many other animals. Beavers are managed as furbearers
and are considered common and abundant throughout their range in Alaska. After mating (which takes
place in January or February), the female prepares for a new litter. Two to four kits, on average, are born
anytime from late April to June. Their eyes are open at birth and the kits are covered with soft fur. They
can swim at 4 days and dive at 2 months of age. The young beavers live with their parents until they are 2
years old. Beavers construct dams and lodges from felled trees, mud, plants, and sticks. Dens may be
constructed in banks or as lodges in slower moving water. Dens and lodges are used for years as a food
cache, rearing area, and home. The life of a beaver colony is determined by food supply. Beavers eat bark,
aquatic plants, roots, and grasses. Once the food supply in an area is exhausted, the beavers must forage
farther from their homes, thus increasing the danger from predators. When an area is cleared of food, the
family migrates to a new home. In Alaska, wolves, lynx, coyotes, bears, and humans are important predators
of beavers according to [26].

3.3.5.3   COMMON MUSKRAT
The muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) are year-round residents throughout most of mainland Alaska south of
the Brooks Range. They are considered widespread and common. They live in small family groups in small
lakes, ponds, marshes, slow streams, sloughs, drainage ditches, and brackish estuaries. Ideal habitat for the
muskrat is permanent wetlands with abundant vegetation that is deep enough to not freeze up in winter.
Muskrats den in burrows and cone-shaped lodges constructed in wet areas. They are primarily herbivorous,
feeding on roots and stems of aquatic plants, but may eat mussels, shrimp, and small fish.
As described in [26], females have two litters per year and give birth to seven to eight young per litter.
Females reach maturity at 9 to 10 months. Young disperse in autumn or spring.

3.3.5.4   MEADOW VOLE

3.3.5.5   NORTH AMERICAN PORCUPINE
Porcupines (Erethizon dorsatum) occur in most of the forested areas in the state. They are solitary and
primarily nocturnal, sleeping in a tree or hollow during the day. Porcupines are chiefly arboreal, feeding on
the inner bark of spruce, birch, and hemlock and spruce needles in winter. They feed on buds and young
green leaves of birch, aspen, cottonwood, and willow in spring and summer. They seek out salt sources,
which can lead to conflicts with humans around outdoor toilets or road maintenance equipment and
facilities. They do not build a nest, but use natural cavities, hollow logs, or thick vegetation as dens.
Breeding takes place in fall and a single porcupette (young porcupine) is born in the spring. Young stay
with their mother during the summer, but are fully weaned and disperse by October. Porcupines can live up
to 18 years in the wild as described by [26].

3.3.5.6   SNOWSHOE HARE
As described in [26], snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus) are distributed over the state except for the lower
Kuskokwim Delta, the Alaska Peninsula, and the area north of the Brooks Range. Snowshoe hares are found
in mixed spruce forests, wooded swamps, and brushy areas. They do not dig burrows or build nests, but use
natural shelters and depressions and rest under branches or bushes. They travel on well-established trails or
runways, which become deeply worn in the snow or forest floor. Winter trails follow the same pathways as
summer trails. Snowshoe hares breed at about 1 year of age and have two to three litters per year. Breeding
begins in mid-May and lasts through August. Gestation is 36 to 37 days. In Interior Alaska, first litters are
born around the middle of May and average about four leverets (young hares). The second litter, in years
of increasing abundance, often averages six young, and occasionally a third litter. They feed on a wide
variety of plant material—grasses, buds, twigs, and leaves in the summer and spruce twigs and needles,
bark, and buds of hardwood such as aspen and willow in the winter. Populations of snowshoe hare are
subject to cycles of high abundance and scarcity. Hare populations will build up over a period of years to
peak abundance with as many as 600 animals per square mile, followed by a sudden decline to a very low
level. Possible reasons for these cycles may include over-browsed food supply, predators, and shock disease
due to stress, parasites, or a combination of these factors.

3.3.5.7   LITTLE BROWN MYOTIS (BAT)
The little brown myotis or bat (Myotis lucifugus) is widely distributed across Alaska in summer. They occur
in numerous habitats, but generally associate with coastal forested habitats and Interior riparian forests.
Bats use echolocation to find and capture insects while hunting at night. The lack of darkness during
summer at high latitudes reduces that amount of time available for foraging. Little brown bats usually mate
during August through October. Ovulation and fertilization are delayed until spring, and gestation lasts 50
to 60 days. Females give birth to a single pup in their first or second year. They may use buildings for roosts
and maternity colonies. Maternity colonies range in size from 70 to 200 in Interior Alaska. The young are
weaned and become capable of flying on their own within about three weeks. In Southeast Alaska, pregnant
females have been captured as early as June 4 and as late as July 2; juvenile bats have been captured or
collected from mid-June through late August. A spike in observations of bats in mid-August suggests young
bats emerge in August in more northern reaches of the state. Whether little brown bats in Interior Alaska
migrate to milder climates to hibernate is unknown. The population size and status of little brown bats in
Alaska is unknown. They are apparently widespread, but in low numbers according to [26].
