3.3.5.8   AMERICAN MARTEN
As described in [26], American martens (Martes americana) are a carnivorous, furbearing member of the
weasel family. Martens are usually found in the uplands and inhabit most forested regions in Alaska. Mating

berries, especially blueberries, small birds, eggs, and vegetation. The population size of American martens
in Alaska is unknown, but populations are likely large because martens are widespread and widely trapped.

3.3.5.9   AMERICAN MINK

preferring saltwater beaches, riparian habits of lakeshores, marshes, and stream banks. Mink breed from
March through April, depending on latitude. In mink and other weasels, the fertilized egg does not attach
to the uterus to develop right away, as in most mammals. Fetal development takes about 30 days to
complete. In most of Alaska, most births occur during June. Litter size varies from 4 to 10 kits. The den is

and deserted by other animals. Mink will eat almost anything they can catch and kill, including fish, birds,

3.3.5.10 CANADA LYNX
As described in [26], Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis) inhabit much of Alaska's forested terrain and use a
variety of habitats, including spruce and hardwood forests, and both subalpine and successional
communities. The best lynx habitat in Alaska occurs where fires or other factors create and maintain a
mixture of vegetation types with an abundance of early successional growth. Mating occurs in March and
early April, and kittens are born about 63 days later under a natural shelter, such as a spruce felled by wind,
a rock ledge, or a log jam. Lynx kittens open their eyes at about 1 month of age, and they are weaned when
2 to 3 years old. Most litters include 2 to 4 kittens, but sometimes as many as six are born and survive. The
production and survival of lynx kittens is strongly influenced by cyclic changes in snowshoe hare and other
small game populations. The primary prey of lynx in most areas is the snowshoe hare, which undergoes an
8 to 11 year cycle of abundance. This cycle appears to be caused by the interaction of hares with their food
and predators. Lynx are considered common in the areas where they occur.

3.3.5.11 COYOTE
Coyotes (Canis latrans) are members of the dog family, averaging 22 to 33 pounds, or about one-third the
size of wolves. Males are slightly heavier than females. Few records of the coyote north of the Yukon River
exist, although they do occur in the area. Portions of the state with the highest densities of coyotes are the
Kenai Peninsula and Matanuska and Susitna valleys. Coyotes breed in January and March. Shortly before
whelping, one or more dens are prepared for the litter. Coyotes give birth to an average of five to seven
blind and helpless pups. Coyotes den in a variety of protected places and frequently take over the dens of
other animals. It is not unusual for coyotes to move their pups to other dens. Family units may begin to
break up as early as August. In Alaska, coyotes are found mostly as mated pairs with an established territory.
In Interior Alaska, territories may be about 15 square miles. Coyotes are absent or scarce where wolves are
abundant, and foxes are similarly less abundant where coyotes are numerous. Coyotes are opportunistic;
snowshoe hares, voles, and carrion compromise the bulk of their diet, while marmots, ground squirrels,
muskrats, fish, insects, and even Dall Sheep are also taken as shown in [26].

3.3.5.12 ERMINE
As described in [26], ermine (Mustela ermine) occur through the Alaska mainland. Ermine pelage is
reddish-brown above and creamy white below in summer, and changes to completely white in winter with
the tip of the tail remaining black in all seasons. Ermine resemble the long-tailed weasel (Mustela freneta)
in general appearance and coloration, but are smaller, have a shorter tail, and have white fur on the inner
side of hind legs. Least weasels (Mustela nivalis) are also similar in appearance to ermine, but are smaller
and do not have any black on the tail. Ermine mate in late spring to early summer. One litter of four to 13
(average of six) young is born, usually in April or May. Females care for young alone. Dens are located in
hollow logs or under logs, stumps, roots, brush piles, or rocks. Snow provides vital insulation against
extreme air temperatures. Ermine are carnivores that consume mainly small mammals, especially voles and
mice. Ermine are adapted to a wide variety of habitats, but prefer wooded areas with thick understory near
watercourses, and often occupy early successional or forest-edge habitats, wet meadows, marshes, ditches,
riparian woodlands, or river bank with high densities of small mammals and adequate subnivean foraging
space. Shrews, rabbits, and occasionally other small mammals may also be taken. Ermine foraging
strategies are particularly well-adapted to northern environments where prolonged snow cover gives small
predators able to access under snow tunnels a competitive advantage, and where voles are most abundant
prey.

3.3.5.13 NORTH AMERICAN RIVER OTTER
The North American river otter (Lontra canadensis) is found throughout mainland Alaska, with the
exception of the area adjacent to the Arctic coast east of Point Lay. River otters in Alaska breed in spring,

about 25 percent smaller than males. Mating can take place in or out of the water. One to six pups (usually

to 13 months. River otters in Alaska hunt on land, in freshwater, and in saltwater. They eat snails, mussels,
clams, sea urchins, insects, crabs, shrimp, octopi, frogs, a variety of fish, and occasionally birds, mammals,
and vegetable matter according to [26].

3.3.5.14 RED FOX
As described in [26], the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is recognized by its reddish coat, its white-tipped tail, and
black “stockings” although many color variations exist. Red foxes prefer broken country, extensive lowland
marshes, and crisscrossed hills and draws. The species is most abundant south of the Arctic tundra, although
they are also present in tundra regions, which it shares with the Arctic fox. Where the ranges of these two
foxes overlap, the red fox is dominant. In these areas, red foxes have been observing digging arctic foxes
out of their dens and killing them. Red foxes breed from February to March. A litter of 4 pups is common,
but litters regularly can be as large as ten. Both parents care for the young. The family remains intact until
autumn and then breaks apart and each animal is on their own. The den is typically a hole in the earth, up
to 20 feet long, usually on the side of a knoll or hill. It may have several entrances. Sometimes foxes dig
their own dens, more often though, they enlarge the home sites of small burrowing animals such as marmots.
Red foxes are omnivorous. Although foxes eat muskrats, squirrels, hares, birds, eggs, insects, vegetation,
and carrion, voles seem to be their preferred food. Foxes cache excess food when available.

3.3.5.15 WOLVERINE
Wolverines (Gulo gulo) are found throughout Alaska, but tend to avoid areas or exist at lower densities
because the habitat is not suitable for denning or is highly developed/used by people. They are solitary
creatures during the majority of the year. Wolverines are almost constantly travelling in search of food. In
general, males have a larger home range than females, and females with kits have a smaller home range
than females without kits. There are seasonal changes in home range size and usage. In Alaska, male home
ranges vary between 200 and 260 square miles. Females typically have a home range of approximately 115
square miles. Home range size and use patterns are thought to be a response to the availability of food
resources or for adult females to the presence of persistent snow cover for denning. Movements of 40 miles
in a day have been documented. Studies in Southcentral Alaska found that wolverines preferred higher
elevations during the summer and lower elevations during the winter due to varying food availability.
Denning areas typically consist of fell fields with deep snow cover. Few wolverines live longer than 5 to 7
years in the wild, although some may survive to 12 or 13 years of age. Primary natural mortality factors
include starvation, being killed by larger predators like wolves, and being killed by other wolverines as
described in [26].

3.3.6.2.1   Bald Eagle
The Bald Eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is a large raptor and the national bird of the United States,
known for its white head and tail and powerful build. Adults measure about 28-40 inches long, with a

Bald eagles nest near large lakes, rivers, and coastal areas, building massive stick nests high in trees or on
cliffs. Pairs typically lay 1-3 eggs, with incubation lasting about 35 days. Both parents care for the young,
which fledge after 10-12 weeks.
Their diet consists mainly of fish, along with waterfowl, small mammals, and carrion. Bald eagles forage
by soaring and swooping to snatch prey from the water’s surface, as well as by scavenging and stealing
food from other birds as described in [28].

3.4       VEGETATION
This section describes the ecoregion and terrestrial and aquatic vegetation communities associated with
the Project components, including the area surrounding the FSRU/Platform. Where possible, the
vegetation resources associated with the FSRU/Platform are described.
All of the surrounding Project area is located in the Cook Inlet Basin Ecoregion. This ecoregion is
characterized by a mix of continental and maritime climates. The area surrounding the Project area is
dominated by spruce and hardwood forests and contains a high concentration of small lakes, bogs, and
swamps according to [31].
3.4.1     OPEN WATER/OFFSHORE
The vegetation and estuarine habitat in Cook Inlet are defined by extreme tides and heavy sediment. The
proposed Project is located in Upper Cook Inlet, which is characterized by intertidal and subtidal mudflats.
Cook Inlet has one of the strongest tides in the world, which results in a constantly shifting sea floor that
prevents plants from taking root. Plant growth is further restricted by the high silt content of Upper Cook
Inlet, which blocks the sunlight required for photosynthesis.
A review of [32], the USFWS National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) identified one habitat classification
within the offshore section of the Project area; marine subtidal unconsolidated bottom (M1UBL). The
M1UBL code describes the offshore marine habitat being high in salinity with minimal vegetation cover.
The unconsolidated bottom refers to the presence of loose particles on the sea floor, a typical characteristic
of the Upper Cook Inlet.
3.4.2     NON-NATIVE AND INVASIVE PLANTS
Non-native plants are species that occur in a particular geographic area where they don’t naturally exist
according to [33]. The term invasive plant refers to non-native species that negatively affect the area to
which they are introduced, whether that was accidentally or intentionally as defined by [34]. These plants
are often aggressive in growth and are very tolerant to a variety of climatic conditions. As shown in [35],
the majority of invasive plant infestations are linked to human-induced activities. While not as historically
prevalent as other areas of Alaska, the area surrounding the Project area has had a variety of non-native and
invasive plant infestations.
There are multiple pathways that work at the Project area that can propagate non-native and invasive plant
species. These possible pathways include:
      •   Contaminated soil and fill material that is brought to the Project area for construction or landscaping
          activities. This material can contain viable seeds or plant fragments of invasive weeds that can later
          sprout.
      •   Accidental transport of seeds of invasive species on equipment and vehicles. Seeds can cling to tire
          treads, vehicle undercarriages, and various construction equipment and then propagate on-site.
An invasiveness ranking system developed by the Alaska Natural Heritage Program is used to illustrate the
potential threat that non-native species found near the Project area pose to surrounding natural areas. The
system assigns each plant an overall invasiveness score ranging from 0 to 100, where 0 indicates a species
that poses no threat to native ecosystems and 100 indicates a species that poses a significant threat as
outlined in [36]. While survey data is limited at the Kustatan Production Facility, there are confirmed
infestations in the Villages of Tyonek and Beluga. At these sites, small infestations of narrowleaf
hawksbeard, oxeye daisy, field sowthistle, white sweetclover, common plantain, common tansy, pineapple
weed, shepherd’s purse, orange hawkweed were recorded as described by [37].

3.4.3     MARINE VEGETATION RESOURCES
A diverse community of algal species inhabits the Cook Inlet, exhibiting a wide range of life histories and
reproductive strategies. Algal persistence differs among species and environmental conditions, with some
species being perennial and others annual or short-lived according to [38]. Algae may reproduce through
sexual, asexual, and vegetative means, and their abundance and diversity typically increase during spring
and summer in response to longer daylight periods as described in [39]. There are over 170 seaweed species
that are known to occur in the Cook Inlet as outlined in [40]. Also shown in [40], the majority of the
macroalgae in the basin occur along nearshore areas that contain suitable rocky substrate for attachment.
Because of this, the distribution of macroalgae in the Cook Inlet is considered patchy. Similar to
macroalgae, species of microalgae in the Cook Inlet typically occur in areas where there are rock substrate
suitable for attachment. During the spring and summer months, diatoms and microflagellates dominate the
landscape, with chrysophytes and dinoflagellates also present according to [40]. Macroalgae, like various
seaweeds can provide substrate for fish and invertebrates, often providing critical habitat in the Cook Inlet.
Eelgrass (Zostera marina) is the dominant seagrass in the Cook Inlet Basin, with most of the documented
populations occurring in the shallow and protected bays of the Lower Cook Inlet. Eelgrass typically occurs
in mud, sand, or gravel substrates in moderately to fully sheltered environments. High turbidity from glacial
and river sediments, along with a long tidal range are the primary factors limiting seagrass expansion in the
Upper Cook Inlet as described in [41].

3.5.1.2    COOK INLET BELUGA WHALE
Beluga whales (Delphinapterus leucas) are small, white Arctic and sub-Arctic toothed whales, known as
"canaries of the sea" for their diverse vocalizations. They are highly social, live in pods, have flexible necks,
lack a dorsal fin (having a ridge instead), and use a bulbous forehead (melon) for echolocation and
communication, adapting to life under ice with thick blubber.
The Cook Inlet beluga whales are a distinct, endangered population of Alaska’s beluga whales. They are year-
round residents of Cook Inlet, using river deltas in Middle/Cook Inlet in summer/fall (most commonly the Beluga
River, Susitna River, Turnagain Arm, and upper Cook Inlet near the Port of Alaska) and deeper waters in winter
(in lower Cook Inlet near Tuxedni Bay, and other locations [wintering grounds are less known]).
Cook Inlet beluga whales have the smallest population of the five Alaska populations, and it is geographically
separated from the other four populations. It is believed that this population was never large, but once consisted
of over 600 individuals. Between 1994 and 1998, the population declined by approximately 50% to 347 belugas-
largely attributed to overharvest. During the 2023 population estimate, scientists estimated that the population
size is between 290 and 386, with a median best estimate of 331 as shown in [43].
Critical habitat for the Cook Inlet beluga whale was designated in 2011 and consists of two main marine areas
in Cook Inlet, Alaska, comprising 3,013 square miles.
    •     Critical Habitat Area 1 (CHA 1) is the northern section of designated critical habitat, encompassing
          all marine waters of Cook Inlet north of a line from Threemile Creek to Point Possession, including key
          river mouths (Susitna, Little Susitna, Chickaloon) and Turnagain Arm and Knik Arm- with a small
          exclusion area near the Port of Alaska. This region is where the belugas typically feed in the summer/fall
          seasons.
    •     Critical Habitat Area 2 (CHA 2) encompasses marine waters in Lower Cook Inlet, from south of line
          from the mouth of Threemile Creek to Point Possession including waters within 2 nautical miles seaward
          of MHW along the western shoreline of Cook Inlet between 60°15.0′ N. and the mouth of the Douglas
          River; all waters of Kachemak Bay east of 151°40.0′ W.; and waters of the Kenai River below the
          Warren Ames bridge in Kenai, Alaska. This region is thought to be an important over-wintering habitat
          for the belugas.
          The Project Area is located in CHA 2.

north of the critical habitat for this species.

3.5.3.1    SHORT-TAILED ALBATROSS
According to [45], the short-tailed albatross (Phoebastria albatrus) spend most of their time at sea. They range

majority feed along continental shelf-break areas east of Honshu, Japan. During non-breeding season, they feed

3.5.4     AMPHIBIANS AND REPTILES
3.5.4.1    LEATHERBACK SEA TURTLE
The Leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) is a large, aquatic reptile whose range extends into North
Pacific waters. They are the widest ranging sea turtle species in the world. 19 leatherback sightings have been
reported in Alaska since 1960. They can tolerate colder temperatures than other sea turtle species due to high oil
content and large body size.
Unlike other sea turtle species, Leatherback sea turtles lack bony plates on its shell. Its carapace is made up of
leathery, oily connective tissue covering loosely interlocking dermal bones. Its shell is mostly black with pinkish
white on the underside. They can weigh over 2000 pounds and can reach 6.5 feet long.
They reproduce every 2-3 years, where a pregnant female lays several nests after mating in adjacent waters.
Average clutch size is 100 eggs. After 60–65 days, the eggs hatch, and the hatchlings emerge from the nest. The
hatchlings are only 2–3 inches long. They will stay in tropical waters until they grow to a carapace length of 100
centimeters.
Leatherback sea turtles feed on soft-bodied pelagic prey including salps and jellyfish. Their mouths are specially

Potential impacts to ESA-listed species during construction would be limited primarily to vessel-based activities

The Cook Inlet beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas) is the ESA-listed species most likely to occur within the
project area. Potential construction-related effects on Cook Inlet beluga whales would be limited to temporary
behavioral disturbance associated with vessel presence, vessel movements, and underwater noise generated by
construction vessels during anchor installation activities.

3.5.5.2     POTENTIAL OPERATIONAL IMPACTS
3.5.5.2.1    Marine Mammals
Operational impacts to ESA-listed marine mammals would be associated primarily with periodic LNG carrier
arrivals and departures and the continued presence of the moored FSRU. LNG carrier visits are anticipated
approximately every 45 to 60 days.
Vessel transits may result in temporary behavioral disturbance, including localized avoidance of vessel routes
and temporary exposure to vessel-generated underwater noise. Because vessel traffic would be infrequent and
would occur within an area already used by commercial and industrial vessels, operational effects are expected
to be minor, localized, and temporary.
The FSRU and mooring system would occupy a relatively small area and are not expected to impede movement
of Cook Inlet beluga whales or substantially alter habitat use patterns. No long-term adverse effects on the Cook
Inlet beluga whale population are anticipated.

temporarily disturb fish in the immediate vicinity of transiting vessels; however, these effects would be localized
and short-lived. Project operations would not be expected to adversely affect fish habitat, migration corridors,
spawning areas, or water quality.

    •     Maintain vessel speeds appropriate for safe navigation and operational requirements.
    •     Comply with all applicable U.S. Coast Guard navigation requirements during vessel transits.
    •     Maintain communication between vessel operators and project personnel regarding wildlife
          observations.
    •     Avoid unnecessary vessel maneuvering and idling where practicable.
    •     Implement spill prevention, control, and response measures to avoid impacts to aquatic habitats and
          species.
    •     Maintain vessels and equipment in good operating condition to minimize the potential for accidental
          releases.
    •     Conduct operations in accordance with all applicable federal permit conditions and consultation
          requirements.
Based on the limited extent of in-water construction, the absence of pile driving and dredging, and the infrequent
vessel traffic associated with project operations, impacts to ESA-listed species are expected to be minor,
localized, and temporary. No significant adverse effects on ESA-listed marine mammals, fish, birds, or sea
turtles are anticipated.
